# Hinagata

> A 3D character engine for the browser (three.js) that makes anime-style characters, tall (the default, about 5 heads) or chibi.
> A character is a recipe: a small JSON object of options, built into a skinned, animated avatar at runtime. Made for vibe coding: you
> (the agent) make the game and give it characters; the user fine-tunes them in the editor at https://hinagata.pages.dev, live, while you
> keep working.

Source: https://github.com/saori-subaru/hinagata (public). Everything below is served from https://hinagata.pages.dev with CORS open.

## First: scale and body

The world's scale comes from what the game is, not from the default character.
- Build the game world at real scale, in metres (a tennis court is 23.77 m long, a door 2 m high, a car 4.5 m). Size the character to the
  game: scale `avatar.object` (an adult about 1.7 m, a child about 1.2 m). Don't shrink the court, the rooms or the camera to the character.
- Use the default body (tall, about 5 heads) unless the user asks for chibi, cute or kids. Then merge a chibi body type (`BODY_TYPES.standard`,
  `.girl`, `.sturdy`, `.toddler`) into the recipe, and then it is fine to scale the world to them (a chibi game).
- Don't make the game look childish unless the user asked for it: the UI, colors, camera and sounds follow what the game is.

```js
import { createAvatar, BODY_TYPES } from "https://hinagata.pages.dev/src/index.js";
const hero = await createAvatar("character.json");                                   // the default body: tall
// const kid = await createAvatar({ ...BODY_TYPES.standard, hair: { back: "bob" } });   // chibi, only when asked for
hero.update(0, { instant: true });                                                    // (posed, so it can be measured)
hero.object.scale.setScalar(1.7 / new THREE.Box3().setFromObject(hero.object).getSize(new THREE.Vector3()).y);   // 1.7 m in a world in metres
```
Measures (`measureGait`, `measureStride`, `measureBody`) are in the avatar's own units: multiply them by `avatar.object.scale.x`.

## The game is the job

The user asked for a game. Make it as good a game as you would with any other 3D characters: the rules, the controls and how they feel,
the camera, the sounds, the screens around it (title, score, results), touch controls if it may run on a phone. That is where your time
goes. The character is one asset among the court, the ball and the UI:
- Start it in a few minutes: colors, a hairstyle, an outfit (`colors`, `hair`, `outfit`; a body type from `BODY_TYPES` if the game
  wants one). Don't keep refining it; the user does the fine-tuning in the editor (below), and you can change the recipe file any time later.
- Don't let the chibi look set the game. Its rules, depth, pace and presentation come from what the user asked for, as they would with
  realistic figures: a tennis game has real tennis in it, a full-size court, a scoreboard. Scale the characters to the world, not the
  world to the characters.
- Don't shape the game around what the engine shows off. If the game needs a move the engine lacks (a racket swing, a serve, a kick),
  pose it on `avatar.joints` (below: a plain joint tree, as your own mannequin would be) and check it in screenshots like any other animation.
- Test the game as a game: play it (a bot pressing keys, at real speed), not only the character.

## The character file and the live link

1. Keep the character in its own file, `character.json`, and have the game load it (`createAvatar("character.json")`). Don't bury it in
   code. One file per character. Write it as the editor exports it: `{ "hinagata": 3, "name": "…", "options": { the recipe } }`.
   `"hinagata"` is the recipe version (the defaults the recipe is written against): 3 = today's (the tall body, about 5 heads). Version 2
   (the first tall body, about 4 heads), version 1 and a file that is only a recipe (no `"hinagata"`: the old chibi defaults) are read with
   the defaults they were made against, so old characters stay as they were. Write new files as version 3.
   A file the user saved from the editor (書き出し → JSON / Export → JSON) works as it is: to put their character in the game, they drop it
   in place of the file.
2. Start the live sync so the user can fine-tune it in the editor while you work on the game (they don't need to ask for it):
   ```sh
   curl -O https://hinagata.pages.dev/sync.mjs        # Node 18+, no dependencies
   node sync.mjs character.json                       # keep it running (in the background); it prints a link
                                                      # (port 8790; --port 8800 for another, e.g. when the game's server is on 8790)
   ```
   Give the user the link it prints (`https://hinagata.pages.dev/editor/?sync=…&key=…`), then go back to the game. Every save you make to
   the file shows in their editor at once, and what they change there is written back into the file (only what differs from the defaults,
   keys sorted): read the file again before you change it (with git, their edits show in `git diff`).
3. Optional, if the user wants you to see the character: run the same helper as an MCP server instead of the plain one (not both: one port):
   `claude mcp add hinagata -- node /abs/path/sync.mjs /abs/path/character.json --mcp`. Tools: `editor_link`, `get_recipe`,
   `update_recipe` ({ set: { "dotted.path": value }, reset: [paths] }), `check_recipe`, `find_options` (by words, Japanese or English) and
   `screenshot` (view: free | front | side | back | face; pose: idle, walk, run, …; needs the editor open from the link).

The sync works when you run on the user's own machine (the editor in their browser reaches 127.0.0.1). A cloud agent can't reach it:
then hand the user an editor link with the character in it instead: `https://hinagata.pages.dev/editor/?o=` + encodeURIComponent(JSON of
the character file, `{ "hinagata": 3, "options": … }`; a bare recipe in a link is read as an old one, with the chibi defaults).

## Use it in a page

```html
<script type="importmap">{ "imports": {
  "three": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.160.0/build/three.module.js",
  "three/addons/": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.160.0/examples/jsm/" } }</script>
<script type="module">
import * as THREE from "three";
import { createAvatar } from "https://hinagata.pages.dev/src/index.js";
const avatar = await createAvatar("character.json"); // a file's URL, a character file object or bare options (a bare object in code is
                                                    // today's: the tall default). async: builds the meshes (in workers; cached in
                                                    // the browser), 1–2 s each the first time
scene.add(avatar.object);                           // a THREE.Group: feet at y = 0, facing +z, about 1.6 units tall (the chibi types
                                                    // about 1.35): scale it to your world in metres (above)
avatar.play("walk");
renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => { avatar.update(clock.getDelta(), { camera }); renderer.render(scene, camera); });
</script>
```
- three.js 0.160.0 (the import map above). Light it like a toon character: a HemisphereLight and a DirectionalLight (the shading is cel-style).
- Inside the hair only the bangs draw lines between their locks; the back hair and tails keep only their outer edge (`outline.hairInner`:
  "front", default; "all" / "none"). That uses the stencil buffer, so keep the renderer's (`new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ stencil: true })`: the default in 0.160, not after 0.163). Without
  one the lines inside the hair simply show.
- Show something while the characters build (a title screen, "loading…"); build several at once with `Promise.all`.
- `avatar.dispose()` when you drop it. Several avatars at once are fine. Scale `avatar.object` to your world (an adult about 1.7 m).
- A complete minimal page: https://hinagata.pages.dev/examples/minimal.html (view its source).

## Keep it fast

A character is built in the browser from its recipe (a second or two each on a laptop, more on a phone) and its hair and cloth are
simulated on the CPU every frame. Budget for both:
- Pass the camera to `update`: `avatar.update(dt, { camera })`. The hair and cloth are then simulated every 2nd or 4th frame when the
  character is small on the screen, and not at all when it is off the screen. Without it they are simulated in full every frame:
  about 5 ms a character, 10–13 with a skirt or long hair, 25–30 with a dress, a cape and long hair (a 2.8 GHz cloud CPU). `avatar.detail`
  says what the last update did; `{ detail: "full" | "half" | "low" | "off" }` sets it yourself.
- `createAvatar(recipe, { quality })`: "game" (default), "lite" (a third to a fifth of the vertices, lighter hair, about half the build
  time: crowds, small characters, phones), "fine" (the sharpest shapes, a nose tip or an elf ear's point, at about the triangles of
  "game", but about 2.5x as long to build the first time; the default for `body.adult`) or "high" (6.8 mm cells unthinned, 2–3x the vertices). Weight at "game": 35–50k vertices, 70–100k triangles.
  `{ simplify: 0.15 }` thins the "game" mesh to that share of the triangles (meshoptimizer, from your import map's "meshoptimizer", else
  jsDelivr). The face is kept as built on top of the share, a skirt or cape is thinned less, and thinning stops before the shape would change
  by more than 1% of a part's size, so you may get more triangles than the share: the body never goes thin or spiky. At 0.15: a tall body in
  a T-shirt and shorts about 23k triangles, a chibi with a grass skirt about 33k (the skirt is a third of it).
- Call `measureGait` / `measureStride` once per avatar after it is built, not every frame.
- Don't update avatars nobody sees for long (or pass the camera: off the screen costs nothing). Headless browsers draw slowly; a real GPU doesn't.

## The recipe

Only what differs from the defaults, nested as the options are (in a character file it is the `"options"`). Example:
```json
{ "hinagata": 3, "name": "Lena", "options": {
  "colors": { "hair": "#f3f1ee", "eyes": "#4fb36a" },
  "body": { "head": { "scale": 0.74 } },
  "hair": { "bangs": "nendo", "back": "long", "tail": { "kind": "side", "side": "L" }, "gradient": { "on": true, "color": "#5fae6a" } },
  "outfit": { "dress": { "on": true, "color": "#f8f6f0" }, "shoes": { "kind": "boots" } } } }
```
- Every option, its type, range or choices, default and what it does (Japanese and English): https://hinagata.pages.dev/options.schema.json
  (`options` by dotted path; `tier: "main"` are the ones the editor shows first). Prefer main options; the rest is fine-tuning.
- Check a recipe: `checkOptions(recipe)` → [{ path, problem }] (empty = fine). In a page it comes from `src/index.js`; in Node (no three.js)
  import it from `https://hinagata.pages.dev/src/schema.js` (or the repository's `src/schema.js`). Unknown keys are ignored by the engine, so
  check: a typo silently does nothing.
- Body types: `import { BODY_TYPES }`: tall `standardTall` (the default), `girlTall`, `sturdyTall`; chibi `standard`, `girl`, `sturdy`,
  `toddler`. Merge one into the recipe (`{ ...BODY_TYPES.girl, hair: … }`); each sets the whole body (torso, limbs, proportions, head size). Proportions: `body.proportion` legs, torso, arms (their own length; null = stretched with the torso, as the chibi), hands, feet, shoulders.
- Ready-made characters: `import { CHARACTERS }` → `createAvatar(CHARACTERS.sylvie.file)` (シルヴィ, an elf girl), `CHARACTERS.astel.file`
  (アステル, a hero boy with sword, shield and cape), `CHARACTERS.lumina.file` (ルミナ, a pretty girl with twin tails and bows) or `CHARACTERS.lumina2.file` (ルミナ v2: the same with a longer face in straight lines). Each is a character file (version 3); copy its `options` into your own file to start from it.
  In the editor: the character list → 「プリセットから作る」.
- Main areas: `colors` (skin, hair, eyes), `body` (proportion, head, torso, thickness, sculpt.ears.elf…), `face` (parts: eyes / brows / mouth
  by id, layout, blush), `hair` (bangs: nendo / hime / side / none, back: short / bob / flip / long, each made of locks or a block: bangsForm / backForm "locks" | "block"; short locks hang off the nape or lie along the head: nape "hang" | "lie"; ahoge, tail, gradient, drawn locks), `outfit` (shirt, pants or skirt, dress, cape, socks, shoes,
  suit (a full-body suit), armor, weapon, extras: animal ears / tail / halo / angel or devil wings; garment parts (src/garments): shirt.sailor (a sailor collar with a line)
  and shirt.scarf, gloves (to the wrist … the shoulder, a cuff band), strings (hip strings over a low skirt), headband (bow: "bunny"), socks.stripes,
  shoes.kind "heelBoots" with shoes.cuff), `accessories` (leaf, gem, flower, star, ball, ribbon, button, anchor, band on a bone), `outline`, `shading`.
- Faces can be drawn: the user does that in the editor (face tab); you can pick part ids (`face.parts`) or expressions with `avatar.setFace("happy")`.
  Ask for the standard names (`EXPRESSION_SET`: normal, happy, sad, angry, surprised): each character shows its own version of them when
  the user has made one in the editor (`face.expressions`, e.g. its own drawn smile), else the stock one; "normal" is the face it was built with.

## Proportions: measure, and fit to numbers

Don't guess the body from a picture by eye: measure the picture (heads tall, the hip joints' and knees' heights as shares of the height),
then fit the body to those numbers and measure it:
```sh
node tools/measure.mjs character.json                          # height, heads tall, chin / shoulders / hip joints / knees / ankles
node tools/measure.mjs character.json --fit heads=6.5,hip=0.5  # the body options that come nearest (--write puts them in the file)
node tools/measure.mjs character.json --to 0.38                # a height on the character (share of its height, or 0.62m) as options take it
```
(in a clone of the repository; the sync helper's MCP tools `measure` and `fit_proportions` do the same when it runs from the repository or
with --engine). In code: `measureCharacter(recipe)` and `fitProportions(recipe, { heads, hip, knee, shoulder, chin, height })` (no
three.js: Node too). Heights in options (a skirt's hem, a sock's top, a collar's back) are in base space, the body before
`body.proportion` stretches it, so a centimetre there can be several on the character: convert with `--to` / `measure.base(y)` instead.
Widths aren't stretched. The height is to the top of the head without the hair, standing in its shoes; heads = height ÷ (top of the head
to the chin). The fit turns `body.head.scale`, `body.proportion.legs` and `.torso` (and `body.adult.knee` on the adult body); start a
chibi from a chibi body type. The user can check it in the editor with a reference picture (its height guides show the same numbers).

## Moving it in a game

- `avatar.play(name)`; `avatar.update(dt, { camera })` every frame. All poses: `import { POSES }` → `Object.keys(POSES)`. Among them: idle, walk, run, sneak,
  crawl, jumpRise, jumpAir, jumpLand, fall, hardLand, climb, climbOver, sitChair, sitChairGirl, sitFloor, hugKnees, wave, cheer, banzai, guard,
  attack (the swing for what the right hand holds: sword, greatsword, axe, spear, staff, or a punch; also attack_<weapon>), hit, stun (stars over the head), down,
  throw, chop, stab, pickUp, carry, carryWalk, push, roll, stumble, knockdown, swim, treadWater, wade, glide, sleep, drink, eat, pant, shiver,
  limp, lookAround, listen, hide, balance. A pose is a function of the avatar's clock; `avatar.play(name)` doesn't reset it. To start a move
  from its beginning: `avatar.play(name); avatar.update(0, { t: 0 })` (`update(dt, { t })` sets the clock to t; later updates go on from
  there). One-shot moves (`ONE_SHOT`: stumble, roll, throw, pickUp, stab, knockdown…) loop over their length: start them that way and switch
  away after `ONE_SHOT[name]` seconds.
- Moving the avatar: move `avatar.object` yourself. So the feet don't slide, play the gait at the speed that matches:
  `const g = measureGait(avatar, "run")` (units / s at playback speed 1; `measureStride(avatar, "walk")` for the walk; measure once after
  createAvatar, it plays the pose to measure) → each frame `avatar.update(dt * v / g)`
  while you move the object `v * dt`. The hair, skirts and capes trail behind by themselves when the object moves.
- Turning: rotate `avatar.object` about y (it faces +z).
- Something in a hand (a racket, a sword, a cup): `avatar.hold(racket, "hand.R", { along: "+y", face: "+z" })`. Model it with its origin
  at the middle of its grip, in the world's units. `along`: its axis that runs through the fist and out past the thumb (forward, with the
  arm hanging: a racket's handle → head); `face`: its axis that faces the way the palm does (the strings, a blade's flat). The hand closes
  on it; `avatar.hold(null, "hand.R")` lets go. Works in every pose. (The engine's own weapons: `outfit.weapon`.)
- Switching to a fast move: `avatar.play(name, { blend: 0 })`. By default a switch eases over about 0.35 s, which softens a swing's start.
- Hands or feet onto a point after the pose: `ik2(avatar.bones, LIMBS["hand.R"], target, pole)` (`import { ik2, LIMBS }`), after `update`.
- Instant changes at runtime (no rebuild): `setColors({ hair, shirt, … })`, `setWorn({ shoes: false })`, `setFace(…)`, `setOutline`,
  `setShading("toon" | "soft" | "smooth" | "flat")`, `setRim({ on, color, width, strength })`, `setGradient`, `setAccessories(list)`,
  `setBands({ "outfit.socks.stripes.color": … })` (the collar's line, the gloves' and boots' cuffs, the stripes). Anything else: build a new avatar from the changed recipe.
- A breeze through the hair: `avatar.update(dt, { camera, wind: [2, 0, 0] })` (m/s, world axes, in the avatar's own size; its own motion streams the hair anyway).

## Your own moves: pose the joints

There's no racket swing, serve or kick built in. Write them on `avatar.joints`: one THREE.Group per joint inside `avatar.object` (not
drawn), set up the way you'd build your own mannequin. The avatar follows them.
```js
const j = avatar.joints;                 // hips, spine, chest, upperChest, neck, head, upperArm / lowerArm / hand / upperLeg / lowerLeg / foot .L/.R
avatar.play("joints", { blend: 0 });     // follow the joints from now on (avatar.play("run") etc. switches back to a built-in move)
// each frame, from the game's state (here a forehand, u: 0 backswing → 1 follow-through)
j.spine.rotation.y = -0.7 + 1.3 * u;     // the upper body turns from the right to the left
j["upperArm.R"].rotation.set(0, -1.0 + 2.4 * u, -1.0);   // the arm out to the side, swung round from behind to across the front
j["lowerArm.R"].rotation.x = -0.4 - 0.5 * u;             // the elbow bends
avatar.update(dt, { camera });
```
- At rest every rotation is 0 and the axes are the world's: the character faces +z, its left is +x, up is +y. The arms hang at the sides
  (a little out from the hips), the legs straight down.
- What the angles do (radians): −x swings an arm or a thigh forward (−π/2: pointing ahead), +x back; an elbow bends with −x on
  `lowerArm`, a knee with +x on `lowerLeg`; z lifts an arm out to the side (+z the left arm, −z the right; about ±π/2: level); y turns
  about the vertical (+y toward the character's left). +x bends the spine, chest, neck or head forward. With three.js's rotation order
  (XYZ) a joint's z is applied first, then y, then x, each about the body's fixed axes: `set(0, y, z)` lifts the arm out, then swings it round.
- `j.hips.position.y`: lower it to crouch. Move and turn the character with `avatar.object` as usual. The collarbones rise by themselves
  with a raised arm.
- Start from a built-in move: `avatar.copyMotion("run", t)` sets every joint to the run at time t (the avatar's clock if left out); then
  change the joints you need (the arm that swings).
- Something to swing: `avatar.hold` (above) puts it in the hand, the right way round.
- Built-in moves are written on the bones themselves (`POSES.name = (t) => ({ b: { "upperArm.R": [x, y, z], … }, y })`, Euler angles per
  bone). The bones' arms rest in an A-pose (44° down from level), so an arm's angles there are easiest found by trying: use the joints.

## Already have a rig? Dress it

If the game already animates its own figures (a mannequin of boxes and capsules, another model), keep that code and dress them:
```js
const avatar = await createAvatar(recipe); scene.add(avatar.object);
const f = avatar.follow({ hips: pelvis, spine, head, "upperArm.L": shL, "lowerArm.L": elL, "hand.L": hL, "upperArm.R": shR, "lowerArm.R": elR,
  "hand.R": hR, "upperLeg.L": hipL, "lowerLeg.L": kneeL, "foot.L": ankleL, "upperLeg.R": hipR, "lowerLeg.R": kneeR, "foot.R": ankleR },
  { root: figure, fit: { height: 1.7 } });   // call it while the figure stands in its rest pose (joints unturned)
f.attach(racket, "hand.R");                  // what the figure held, now in the avatar's hand, placed as it was
// each frame, after the game has posed the figure: avatar.update(dt, { camera })
```
Every update copies the figure's joint turns and place onto the avatar and hides the figure. The figure's joints can be any Object3Ds;
their turns are measured from the rest pose they had when follow was called (arms straight down, a T-pose, the avatar's A-pose: all
fine). `fit`: `{ height }` in the figure's units, or true (default) to match the leg length. `grip: { L, R }` closes the hands (0–1).
A figure with one spine joint has its turn shared over the avatar's spine, chest and upper chest; collarbones rise with raised arms.

## Missing a part? Add one

First look for it: `find_options` (or docs/options.schema.json) by words, Japanese or English; `accessories` (small pieces on a bone:
a button, a ribbon, a gem…) cover many details. What the character holds or what floats beside it (a pet, a turret, rigging) is the
game's own three.js, put on a bone (`avatar.bones["hand.R"].add(…)`) or beside the avatar: not a part. A garment the engine lacks (a collar, gloves, a
headband: 島風's were made this way) is a part, one file in your own copy of the engine:
1. `git clone https://github.com/saori-subaru/hinagata`, add `src/garments/<name>.js` and one line in `src/garments/index.js`
   (`import "./<name>.js";`). The part brings its options (with defaults), their names and ranges for the editor's panels, its color
   (`avatar.setColors({ <name>: "#…" })`), putting it on and off (`setWorn`), and its place in the mesh cache:
   ```js
   import { definePart } from "./registry.js";
   const L = (ja, en) => ({ ja, en });
   definePart({ src: import.meta.url, name: "choker", path: "outfit.choker", section: L("チョーカー", "Choker"),
     defaults: { on: false, color: "#202020", width: 0.012 },
     schema: [["on", L("チョーカー", "Choker")], ["color", L("色", "Color"), { when: { ".on": true } }],
              ["width", L("幅", "Width"), { when: { ".on": true }, min: 0.004, max: 0.03, step: 0.001, help: L("m", "m") }]],
     build: ({ O, J, bodySdf }) => { const y = J.neck[1] + 0.03;   // built only while on: the shapes, once per build
       return { sdf: (x, yy, z) => Math.max(bodySdf(x, yy, z) - 0.004, Math.abs(yy - y) - O.width / 2) }; },   // the body 4 mm out, cut to a band
     spec: (st, { H }) => ({ sdf: st.sdf, lo: [-0.1, 0.7, -0.1], hi: [0.1, 0.95, 0.12], h: Math.min(H, 0.004), only: /^(neck|upperChest|head)/ }),
   });
   ```
   Every field is described at the top of `src/garments/registry.js`; `src/garments/` has five real parts to copy from (sailor.js: a
   collar over the shirt with a painted line; gloves.js; strings.js: a strap made directly as a mesh; headband.js: on the hair, in head space).
2. The shape is a signed distance (m; negative inside) in base space: the body before `body.proportion` stretches it (y up, z forward,
   the character's left at +x; the neck about 0.74, the shoulders 0.73, the hips 0.44 there). `build`'s ctx gives the joints `J`
   (`J.neck`, `J["upperArm.L"]`, …), `bodySdf`, `shirtSdf(x, y, z, B, noBell, noHole)`, the body's pieces `P`, and `slope(y)`: how many
   times a height is stretched there (it depends on the body: a band 1 cm tall in base space is slope(y) cm on the character).
   A garment is easiest as what it lies on pushed out a few mm and cut to its region (a solid: only its outside shows).
3. `spec`: the box it is meshed in (`lo`, `hi`, base space), the cell `h` (at most half its thinnest feature: thinner came out in dashes),
   the bones it follows (`only`: a regexp of bone names; or `bone1` for one), `make` to build a mesh directly (a strap a few mm wide).
   `thin: "cloth" | "keep"` keeps a small part from being thinned away at the "fine" / "lite" qualities.
4. Check it: `node tools/schema.mjs` (the options' schema; then `check_recipe` knows them), `node tools/thin-check.mjs` (the thinned
   builds keep their shape; exits 1 if not), and look at it in the editor: `node tools/sync.mjs character.json --engine .` (from the clone) gives
   a link that opens the site's editor running your engine; your part has its section in the Outfit tab. Reload the editor after editing
   the part. Keep the part generic (options); the character's own values go in its file.

## The editor

https://hinagata.pages.dev (the editor) — the user's tool: sliders for every main option, dragging hair tufts and tails on the head,
drawing locks of hair and face parts, painting on the clothes, accessories by clicking, poses to preview, export to code or GLB.
A reference picture can be put over or beside the character at its size, with height guides (its chin, shoulders, hips, knees as
shares of its height, and how many heads tall it is): when the user has a picture of the character they want, suggest it.
`?o=<character file JSON>` opens a character as a new one; `?sync=<port>&key=<key>` (the sync helper's link) follows a file. New
characters there start tall; the body type row offers the chibi ones.
